unused.why: No use since server start or the last change to this table's indexes (COUNT_STAR = 0 in performance_schema.table_io_waits_summary_by_index_usage).
unused.caveat: Make it invisible first and run a full business cycle (month-end jobs, reports, replicas) before dropping it: an invisible index is still maintained on writes, but the optimizer stops using it, and making it visible again is instant. Queries with an index hint that names it fail while it is invisible.

unused.why: Performance Schema shows no use since server start or the last change to this table's indexes, but user statistics (information_schema.INDEX_STATISTICS) count 3 rows read through it since userstat was turned on or the last FLUSH INDEX_STATISTICS, so it is in use. User statistics count every session, including sessions setup_actors does not instrument, and keep their counts when the table is rebuilt; keep it.

notes: Unused means no row read, written or looked up through the index since the server started (8 min 9 s ago), or since an index on that table was added, dropped or renamed, or the table was renamed or rebuilt by copying, any of which restarts its counts. An index used only by a weekly or monthly job looks unused until the job runs.

Tables with no row read or written since the counts started (never opened, or opened only to read their definition) are listed under No data, never as unused. A TRUNCATE of a Performance Schema summary table also resets the counts.

User statistics are on (userstat=ON), so an index that Performance Schema shows unused but information_schema.INDEX_STATISTICS shows read is marked keep. They count from when userstat was turned on or the last FLUSH INDEX_STATISTICS.
Percona Server's user statistics do not support partitioned tables, so for the 2 partitioned tables in scope they can show that an index was read, never that it was not.
The server has been up only 8 min 9 s, so infrequent jobs may not have run yet.

PRIMARY and UNIQUE indexes are never listed as unused: they enforce constraints even when no query reads them. Indexes that back a foreign key are marked keep: InnoDB checks foreign keys without going through the usage counters.
Foreign keys declared in other schemas that reference review are not checked; a non-unique parent index they use could look unused.
Counts are per server: reads on replicas are not included.
